item.title: How to Cancel a Solar Contract: Cooling-Off Rights by State
item.description:
Most solar cancellations do not blow up because the customer changed their mind. They blow up because nobody wrote anything down, the deposit sat in the business account, and a polite “actually, we’ve decided not to go ahead” got treated as a maybe instead of a legal notice.

I have watched this play out from every side of the trade: sitting across the kitchen table on a quote, sitting in a supplier’s office when a deal fell over, and sitting with business owners trying to work out whether they had to give a deposit back. So this one is written for you, the operator. If you understand exactly what your customer is entitled to when they want out, you can handle the cancellation cleanly, keep it off the Clean Energy Council’s desk, and move on. Get it wrong and a two-minute phone call becomes a tribunal claim.

item.title: Best E-Signature Software for Solar Contracts in Australia
item.description: Search “best e-signature software Australia” and you get a wall of comparison pages built for any small business: accountants, real estate agents, gyms. They rank on the same three things every time, data residency, price in Australian dollars, and how many templates you get. Useful if you are a bookkeeper. Close to useless if you are a solar retailer, because not one of them mentions the documents that actually carry legal risk in this trade: the mandatory disclosure statement, the cooling-off cancellation notice, and the STC assignment form.

item.title: Solar Installer Goes Bust: Protect Your Deposit
item.description: Every year a handful of solar businesses go under, and every time it happens the same thing plays out. Customers who paid a deposit, or worse paid in full before the panels went up, are left holding nothing. Then the phones ring at every surviving installer in the area, because those stranded customers need someone to finish the job or fix a fault, and they are now wary of handing a deposit to anyone ever again.
